strategy_title: maxnreg Cap + block_ptr Causes Local-Memory Spill Regression
strategy_description: Capping registers via maxnreg=64 (down from 150) while switching to tl.make_block_ptr caused a 1.82x slowdown (duration 66.5→121.6 µs). Although theoretical occupancy improved (18.75%→37.5%) and L1 hit rate jumped dramatically (2.66%→70.31%), achieved occupancy remained identical at 6.25% and executed instructions increased by 38% (10.2M→14.1M). The new MemoryCacheAccessPattern rule flagged severe uncoalesced local loads/stores (only 1 of 32 bytes per sector utilized), indicating the register cap forced spills to local memory, which introduced high-latency L1TEX stalls (40.4% of cycles) that more than offset the bank-conflict reduction. The anti-pattern is applying maxnreg aggressively on a kernel where the register file is genuinely needed — forced spills to local memory are far more expensive than the occupancy gain from freeing register slots.
fast_pseudocode:
# After: 64 regs/thread (spills!), block_ptr, 121.6 µs — SLOWER
@triton.autotune(configs=[Config(num_warps=4, num_stages=3, maxnreg=64), ...], key=[])
def kernel(...):
    b_block_ptr = tl.make_block_ptr(base=B, shape=(N,K),
        strides=(stride_bn, stride_bk), offsets=(pid_n*BLOCK_N, k_idx*BLOCK_K),
        block_shape=(BLOCK_N, BLOCK_K), order=(1,0))
    b = tl.load(b_block_ptr, boundary_check=(0,1), padding_option='zero')
    acc += tl.dot(a, tl.trans(b))
applicable_when: Never apply maxnreg to cap registers below what the compiler naturally allocates when the kernel has a large accumulator tile (e.g. 64x64 FP32 = 4096 elements). The register pressure is genuine and spills will be worse than low occupancy.
do_not_apply_when: Do not apply maxnreg register capping when: (1) the kernel has a large accumulator tile that genuinely requires many registers; (2) the MemoryCacheAccessPattern rule is not already present before the change (its appearance after indicates spills); (3) achieved occupancy does not improve despite theoretical occupancy improving — this signals the bottleneck is not occupancy-limited but instruction-count or latency-limited.
framework_notes: In Triton, maxnreg in triton.Config caps the maximum registers per thread. When set too low relative to the kernel's natural register demand, the compiler spills to local memory (thread-private DRAM-backed storage), causing uncoalesced local load/store traffic visible as MemoryCacheAccessPattern NCU rule. This is distinct from shared memory bank conflicts. The tl.make_block_ptr change itself (without maxnreg) may still be beneficial for coalescing — the regression is primarily attributable to the register cap causing spills.

strategy_title: Direct [K,N] B-tile Load Causes Local-Memory Spill Regression
strategy_description: Replacing tl.make_block_ptr + tl.trans(b) with scalar pointer arithmetic loading B as [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N] directly, combined with maxnreg=64, caused a 1.95x slowdown (duration 66.98→129.95 µs). Although theoretical occupancy improved (18.75%→37.5%) and L1 hit rate jumped dramatically (2.66%→71.05%), achieved occupancy remained identical at 6.25% and executed instructions increased by 40% (10.2M→14.2M). The new MemoryCacheAccessPattern rule flagged severe uncoalesced local loads/stores (only 1 of 32 bytes per sector utilized), indicating the maxnreg=64 cap forced register spills to local memory, introducing high-latency L1TEX stalls (41.7% of cycles) that more than offset any bank-conflict reduction. The root cause of the regression is the same as iteration 4: aggressively capping registers via maxnreg on a kernel with a large accumulator tile causes spills that are far more expensive than the original shared memory bank conflicts.
slow_pseudocode:
# Before: 158 regs/thread, 12-way shared bank conflicts, 66.98 µs
@triton.autotune(configs=[Config(num_warps=4, num_stages=3), ...], key=[])
def kernel(...):
    b_block_ptr = tl.make_block_ptr(B, shape=(N,K), strides=(stride_bn,stride_bk),
        offsets=(pid_n*BLOCK_N, k_idx*BLOCK_K), block_shape=(BLOCK_N,BLOCK_K), order=(1,0))
    b = tl.load(b_block_ptr, boundary_check=(0,1), padding_option='zero')  # [BLOCK_N, BLOCK_K]
    acc += tl.dot(a, tl.trans(b), allow_tf32=ALLOW_TF32, out_dtype=ACC_TYPE)
fast_pseudocode:
# After: 64 regs/thread (spills!), scalar ptr, no tl.trans, 129.95 µs — SLOWER
@triton.autotune(configs=[Config(num_warps=4, num_stages=3, maxnreg=64), ...], key=[])
def kernel(...):
    k_global = k_idx * BLOCK_K + offs_k   # [BLOCK_K]
    b_ptrs = B + k_global[:, None] * stride_bk + offs_b_n[None, :] * stride_bn
    b_mask = k_global[:, None] < K
    b = tl.load(b_ptrs, mask=b_mask, other=0.0)  # [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N]
    acc += tl.dot(a, b, allow_tf32=ALLOW_TF32, out_dtype=ACC_TYPE)
applicable_when: Never: this approach of eliminating tl.trans via direct [K,N] scalar pointer load combined with maxnreg capping consistently causes register spills that are worse than the original bank conflicts in this kernel class.
do_not_apply_when: Do not apply maxnreg register capping (e.g. maxnreg=64) when the kernel has a large accumulator tile (e.g. 64x64 FP32 = 4096 elements) that genuinely requires many registers. The MemoryCacheAccessPattern NCU rule appearing after the change (with only 1/32 bytes per sector utilized for local loads/stores) is a definitive signal that spills occurred and the approach caused regression. Also do not apply when achieved occupancy fails to improve despite theoretical occupancy improving — this signals the bottleneck is not occupancy-limited.
framework_notes: In Triton, maxnreg in triton.Config caps the maximum registers per thread. When set too low relative to the kernel's natural register demand (here 158 regs), the compiler spills to local memory (thread-private DRAM-backed storage), causing uncoalesced local load/store traffic visible as MemoryCacheAccessPattern NCU rule. This is the same failure mode as iteration 4 (item b7c2f441). Eliminating tl.trans by loading B as [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N] directly is mathematically correct but does not help if the register cap causes spills. The shared memory bank conflicts (12-way, 77.67% of loads) remain essentially unchanged between before and after, confirming the tl.trans elimination alone did not fix the bank conflict pattern in this kernel.
